sections.html:
• Origin: Cosmopolitan
  • Growth rate: Medium
  • Height: 10-15+ cm (average height after two months in the tank)
  • Light demand: Low
  • CO2: Low

• Common name: Dwarf hairgrass (DHG, needle spikerush, needle spikesedge, spikerush)
  • Scientific name: Eleocharis sp. (Eleocharis acicularis, Eleocharis parvula, Eleocharis Belem (mini))
  • Minimum tank size: 10 litres
  • Difficulty: easy to medium
  • Lighting: moderate to high
  • Substrate: soft substrate
  • Growth rate: low to moderate
  • Placement: foreground
  • Fertilizers: highly recommended
  • CO2: highly recommended
  • Propagation: by runners
  • Colour: green

Eleocharis acicularis belongs to the genus Eleocharis in the family Cyperaceae, a family of grass-like monocotyledonous flowering plants known as sedges. The name acicularis is of Latin origin and means 'needle-shaped'.

Dwarf hairgrass is widespread and has a cosmopolitan distribution. It grows in the temperate, subtropical and tropical zones of the world, excluding Africa.
Dwarf hairgrass can be found on the banks or edges of slow-moving rivers, lakes, ponds, marshes and swamps.
Dwarf hairgrass can thrive in a variety of tank sizes, even nano tanks if properly maintained. The recommended minimum tank size is about 40 litres. Ideally use a shallow tank so the light is strong.

Eleocharis acicularis is very common and thrives in almost all conditions in an aquarium. An open space without shading from other plants is still preferable. After planting, the roots will start colonizing the surroundings, creating a beautiful carpet of 6-15 cm height. If the carpet grows too tall, you may carefully cut it back to the preferred height.

Dwarf hairgrass is fairly easy to maintain. Although it carpets through dense horizontal growth, it can also grow vertically, so trim it regularly for a carpet look. Regular trimming stimulates horizontal growth by promoting runners. Clip the top shoots to keep it compact.

If growth is painfully slow, trim it to about 2.5 cm from the substrate; this significantly increases growth rate. Otherwise it spends its energy growing toward the light.

Occasionally brush the carpet with tweezers to stir debris up to the surface, as a dense carpet easily becomes clogged with debris.

Planting

  • Split the clump into portions of 1–4 blades (the fewer the better). Planting the whole clump together may not yield healthy plants (the centre often dies) or the desired carpet.
  • Clipping the existing roots prompts new roots to grow, which helps the carpet spread rapidly.
  • Use tweezers to gently place portions into the substrate. Keep the whole strands above the substrate, with only the roots beneath. The plant tends to float and is fine to hold down, so it may be tricky at first.
  • Space portions 2.5–5 cm apart to avoid overcrowding and promote uniformity.
  • Fertilize adequately and trim to the desired height when needed. Trimming when planting makes the roots grow stronger.

Propagation

You cannot cut and replant a stem to get a new plant. Propagation is by runners that emerge and branch off laterally from the base of the stem. Make sure the plants get enough light, CO2 and nutrients to promote prolific runners.

Dry start method

  • Instead of filling the tank right after planting, add only enough water to reach the surface of the lowest part of the substrate.
  • Use tweezers to plant the hairgrass and sprinkle it on top of the substrate.
  • Cover the top of the tank with cling wrap to increase humidity.
  • After about 5 to 8 weeks you can flood the tank.

This method provides unlimited CO2 at no cost and allows growing the plant even before cycling the tank.

• Temperature: tolerates and thrives in a wide range, even cool water of 10 °C, but 22–26 °C is ideal.
  • pH: not suited to extreme pH; keep it between 6.5 and 7.5 for best growth.
  • Hardness: soft to moderately hard water; 2–10 GH is great.

Lighting

Dwarf hairgrass needs ample light to form a nice carpet and attains a rich green colour under moderate to high lighting. Use LED lighting for at least 8–10 hours daily. Watch for algae and adjust the lights accordingly.

Substrate

Although it prefers a nutrient-rich substrate, it also grows well in sand. The fine grains let the thin roots penetrate. Avoid coarse gravel. A soft substrate is better because the roots are thin, weak and prone to damage. The carpet effect is also easier to achieve on sand because the runners spread well. You can spread a layer of nutrient-rich aqua soil beneath the sand. Fertilizers are needed with a sand substrate, as sand contains no nutrients.

CO2 and fertilization

The plant needs a great deal of nutrients and CO2. CO2 injection speeds up fast, dense carpet growth and gives a vibrant green colour. It can grow without CO2, but the spread is much slower: it can take a month or more to catch on and several more months to get going.

If the water column has good nutrient levels, the plant takes them up from there, so liquid fertilizers and root tabs both work. Bright light and sufficient nutrients boost growth. Without CO2, the more light there is, the more algae there will be, so balance light, CO2 and nutrients.

If you keep shrimp with dwarf hairgrass, note that high CO2 levels and copper (contained in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Dwarf hairgrass is a grass-like plant that grows in rosettes. It has a rich green colour that deepens under bright lighting. Depending on the species, it reaches a height of up to 5–15 cm with long, hair-like blades that are quite upright and stringy.

Eleocharis acicularis is sometimes confused with Eleocharis parvula or Eleocharis Belem (sp. mini), and is often mislabelled as one or the other. They are not the same.

  • Eleocharis acicularis grows a little taller and more upright.
  • Eleocharis parvula looks similar but is shorter (8–10 cm) and the shoots tend to spread more. The leaf blade is like a straight sword.
  • Eleocharis Belem (mini) is the smallest dwarf hairgrass in the hobby. It usually starts to arch toward the ground and reaches 3–4 cm tall.

Benefits

  • Aquascape: forms a dense, lush green carpet and can be placed in different areas of the aquarium.
  • Shelter: acts as shelter for bottom-dwelling fish and fry.
  • Oxygenation: helps oxygenate the tank water.
  • Breeding ground: serves as a breeding place for egg scatterers and a foraging ground for shrimp and juvenile fish.
  • Removal of excess nutrients: capable of absorbing heavy metals and toxins from the water.
  • Prevents gas pockets: the root system helps break up anaerobic pockets in the substrate. Hydrogen sulfide pockets (H2S, smells like rotten eggs) can be really dangerous to fish or shrimp.

Problems

  • Melting: at first the plant may wither, probably because it was grown emersed and the transition to submersed growth is stressful. It takes time to recover and adapt.
  • Algae: highly susceptible to algae, especially hair algae, caused by poor water quality, low CO2, excess light and nutrients. Adjust lighting intensity, do regular water changes and introduce algae-eaters.
  • Slow growth: after planting it often does nothing noticeable for a month or more while it develops its root system.
  • Discoloration: blades turning brown or yellow patches result from nutrient deficiencies. Yellow spots likely point to a lack of iron, while brown colouration is due to a lack of macronutrients. Supply supplements rich in iron and macronutrients in the right dosage.

Tankmates

Because of its thin, stringy blades, most fish do not find it palatable, so it can be kept with a variety of species.

  • Fish: Corydoras catfish, neon tetras, ember tetras, guppies, mollies, Otocinclus, pygmy corydoras, etc.
  • Shrimp: cherry shrimp, snowball shrimp, Caridina cf. babaulti, ghost shrimp, Amano shrimp, blue tiger shrimp, blue velvet shrimp, vampire shrimp, bamboo shrimp, cardinal shrimp, red nose shrimp, etc.
  • Snails: Japanese trapdoor snails, ramshorn snails, nerite snails, Malaysian trumpet snails, black devil snails, Asolene spixi, rabbit snails, etc.

Avoid large, aggressive, digging and plant-eating fish that will tear up the plant, such as goldfish, oscars, rainbowfish, Jack Dempsey and clown loaches. Most crayfish and freshwater crabs are also a poor combination, as they cut, eat and uproot everything in the tank.

Buying

This Eleocharis is readily available in local fish stores and is inexpensive, usually sold as a clump wrapped in rock wool. Pick healthy plants with bright green blades; unhealthy ones have brown colouration, visible patches or algae. Avoid specimens bending to the side; a healthy plant should be firm and upright.

You can also place clumps beside rocks and driftwood for a visually appealing effect.
